name: Baotou Donghe International Airport
before:
Baotou's airport in Inner Mongolia, about 14 miles from the city, and one of the oldest airfields still flying in China. It was built in 1934 by the Eurasia Aviation Corporation, a joint venture between the Chinese government and Lufthansa, and handled four seat aircraft cruising at 165 kilometres an hour. It was occupied by Japan during the Second World War.

The name has changed repeatedly, which matters when searching supplier systems. It began as Hailanpao, became Erliban in 1956, was renamed Baotou Donghe in March 2018 and became Baotou Donghe International in October 2024.

International flying is very recent. The first international route only opened in August 2016, when Mongolian Hun Airlines began flying a Fokker F50 between Ulaanbaatar and Baotou, and full approval to operate internationally came in November 2019.

Terminal T1 dates from 1999 and T2 opened in December 2014. The runway was extended to 2,800 metres in 2006.
after:
Baotou's airport in Inner Mongolia, about 14 miles from the city. It has a long history: it was built in 1934 by the Eurasia Aviation Corporation, a joint venture between the Chinese government and Lufthansa.

The name has changed repeatedly, which matters when searching supplier systems. It was Erliban until March 2018 and Baotou Donghe until October 2024, when it became Baotou Donghe International.

International flying is very recent. The first international route opened in August 2016, when a Mongolian airline began flying a Fokker 50 between Ulaanbaatar and Baotou under a temporary opening. State Council approval came in November 2019, and the airport formally opened to international traffic in December 2023, after a national inspection.

The runway was extended to 2,800 metres in 2006, and Terminal T2 opened in December 2014.

claims.claim: first international route in August 2016: a Mongolian airline's Fokker 50 from Ulaanbaatar, under a temporary opening
claims.inAfter: The first international route opened in August 2016, when a Mongolian airline began flying a Fokker 50 between Ulaanbaatar and Baotou under a temporary opening.
claims.note: Was 'when Mongolian Hun Airlines began flying a Fokker F50'. CAOP names the airline only in Chinese (蒙古国匈奴航空) and 'Mongolian Hun Airlines' is Wikipedia's rendering, so the text says 'a Mongolian airline'. The temporary opening ran from 1 July to 31 December 2016 (CAOP, Wikipedia); Xinhua (2024) counts 12 international routes opened over seven temporary openings.

On 3 August of the same year, the airport opened its first international route. Mongolian Hun Airlines used Fokker F50 aircraft to fly the round-trip route from Ulaanbaatar to Baotou.

claims.note: Was 'full approval to operate internationally came in November 2019'. The State Council approved the opening in November 2019, but the port of entry opened formally only after the national port office's inspection on 23 December 2023 (Xinhua, Wikipedia).

On 23 December 2023, the Baotou Donghe Airport air port opened to the outside world and passed national acceptance.

claims.why: Wikipedia alone; CAOP's history goes from 1934 to 1956 without it.

claims.wasBefore: It began as Hailanpao, became Erliban in 1956
claims.why: Both the Hailanpao name and the 1956 date of the Erliban name rest on Wikipedia alone (CAOP gives 1956 only as the year the civil aviation Baotou station was set up). Erliban itself is kept (see above).

claims.wasBefore: Mongolian Hun Airlines began flying a Fokker F50
claims.why: The English airline name is Wikipedia's rendering of 匈奴航空 and no source here gives the airline's own English name, so 'a Mongolian airline'. The aircraft is the Fokker 50 (CAOP: 福克50).

claims.claim: full approval to operate internationally came in November 2019
claims.wasBefore: full approval to operate internationally came in November 2019
claims.why: Misleading: November 2019 was the State Council's approval (kept), but the port of entry opened formally only on 23 December 2023, after the national inspection (see above).

The 1999 date rests on Wikipedia alone. CAOP names T1 as the international terminal and T2 as the domestic one, and Xinhua (2024) says the old terminal was rebuilt as the international terminal between 2014 and 2017; neither dates T1, and neither is within 12 months, so the split is not added either.

claims.note: CAAC: 1,965,255 passengers in 2025 against 2,164,827 in 2024 (down 9.2 per cent), 80th in China and fourth in Inner Mongolia after Hohhot, Hailar and Ordos; Wikipedia's infobox gives the same 2025 figure.
